narrative: Today's strongest thread is disturbance and its downstream reshuffling of communities: analysis of Australia's Black Summer bushfires shows biodiversity-focused actions can be woven into emergency response, while simulated forest landscapes reveal how slowed regeneration and climate change can lock temperate forests into self-reinforcing fire-trap feedbacks. A global assessment of nearly 9,800 freshwater fish species finds warming triggers abrupt thermal exposure that is accelerating habitat fragmentation, especially in the tropics, and drought is shown to intensify how carnivores avoid dominant competitors when selecting habitat. Invasive species keep restructuring trophic architecture: non-native fish alter predator-prey mass ratios in freshwater communities, invasive goldfish trigger regime shifts in experimental lakes, and reduced litter allelochemicals from one alien plant invader appear to facilitate further invasions. On the recovery side, 38 years of rewetting forestry-drained temperate fens is restoring both peat accumulation and near-natural vegetation. Several new machine-learning tools for passive acoustic monitoring - including zero-shot call classifiers and contrastive soundscape embeddings - are expanding automated species detection, and a new eco-evolutionary model identifies competing selective forces behind how pathogens time their seasonal epidemics.
